subtopic_detail: Smoking cessation pharmacotherapy with a psychiatric history
stem:
You are the registrar in a general practice clinic seeing a 44 year old woman who smokes 30 cigarettes a day and has done so since she was 17. She wakes at night to smoke and lights her first cigarette within five minutes of waking.

She has tried nicotine patches alone twice and relapsed within a fortnight on both occasions. She has a history of a single depressive episode eight years ago, treated with sertraline and in full remission for seven years off all medication. She has no history of seizures, no eating disorder and no current depressive symptoms. Her renal function and liver function are within normal limits.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 76, BP 130/82, RR 15, SpO2 97% room air, temperature 36.6
data_table.Examination: Euthymic, no suicidal ideation, no cognitive impairment
data_table.Investigations: Renal function, liver function, full blood count and thyroid function within normal limits

lead_in: Which pharmacotherapy is the most appropriate first choice?

options.text: Nicotine patch 21 mg daily used alone for 12 weeks with behavioural support
options.rationale: Single form nicotine replacement has already failed twice in a heavily dependent smoker, so repeating it without escalation is unlikely to succeed a third time (Source: RACGP Supporting Smoking Cessation guideline).

options.text: Bupropion 150 mg daily for three days then twice daily for nine further weeks
options.rationale: Bupropion is less effective than varenicline in head to head comparison and lowers the seizure threshold, so it sits behind varenicline rather than ahead of it (Source: RACGP Supporting Smoking Cessation guideline; Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Varenicline titrated over the first week and continued for 12 weeks after quitting
options.rationale: Varenicline is the most effective single agent for smoking cessation, and a large randomised safety trial found no excess neuropsychiatric events in people with treated and stable psychiatric illness (Source: RACGP Supporting Smoking Cessation guideline; Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Nicotine lozenges used as required alone for 12 weeks with behavioural support
options.rationale: Oral nicotine alone provides less consistent coverage of background craving than a patch, so it is weaker rather than stronger than the strategy that has already failed (Source: RACGP Supporting Smoking Cessation guideline).

options.text: Behavioural counselling and quitline referral alone with no pharmacotherapy offered
options.rationale: Behavioural support roughly doubles quit rates but withholding pharmacotherapy from a heavily dependent smoker forfeits the larger part of the achievable benefit (Source: RACGP Supporting Smoking Cessation guideline).

explanation.summary: Time to first cigarette under 30 minutes and waking overnight to smoke are the two most useful bedside markers of heavy nicotine dependence and both predict that monotherapy with a patch will fail. Varenicline is the most effective single pharmacotherapy, with combination nicotine replacement using a patch plus an oral form as the closest alternative. Historical concerns about varenicline causing neuropsychiatric harm were largely resolved by a large randomised trial that found no excess of such events in people with stable psychiatric illness, and a boxed warning was subsequently removed in several jurisdictions. Remitted depression is therefore not a reason to avoid varenicline, though monitoring mood during a quit attempt remains sensible because nicotine withdrawal itself lowers mood.
key_points: Smoking within 30 minutes of waking and overnight smoking mark heavy dependence
Varenicline is the most effective single agent and combination nicotine replacement is the closest alternative
Randomised safety data found no excess neuropsychiatric events in stable psychiatric illness
Behavioural support roughly doubles quit rates and is combined with, not substituted for, pharmacotherapy
explanation.pearls: Start varenicline one to two weeks before the nominated quit date and keep smoking during the titration, because the quit date is set after steady state is reached rather than on the first day of treatment.

subtopic_detail: Alcohol use disorder pharmacotherapy with hepatic impairment
stem:
You are the registrar in a hospital drug and alcohol service reviewing a 55 year old man three days after an admission for decompensated alcohol related liver disease. He has completed uncomplicated withdrawal management and is now medically stable.

He has been drinking about 20 standard drinks daily for 15 years and states that his goal is complete abstinence. His most recent imaging and bloods confirm established cirrhosis with a bilirubin of 46 micromol/L, an albumin of 29 g/L and an international normalised ratio of 1.6. He takes no opioids and has no renal impairment. He has never taken pharmacotherapy for alcohol use disorder.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 82, BP 118/70, RR 16, SpO2 97% room air, temperature 36.7
data_table.Examination: Palmar erythema, spider naevi, no asterixis, no ascites on examination
data_table.Investigations: Bilirubin 46 micromol/L (less than 20); albumin 29 g/L (35-50); international normalised ratio 1.6 (0.9-1.3); creatinine 74 micromol/L (60-110)

lead_in: Which pharmacotherapy is the most appropriate choice to support abstinence?

options.text: Naltrexone 50 mg daily commenced now and continued for at least six months
options.rationale: Naltrexone undergoes extensive hepatic metabolism and is avoided in acute hepatitis and decompensated liver disease, which is the situation here (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook; Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction Medicine).

options.text: Disulfiram 200 mg daily commenced now and continued with supervised dosing
options.rationale: Disulfiram is hepatotoxic in its own right and is contraindicated in significant hepatic impairment, so it is the least safe option in a decompensated patient (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Diazepam 5 mg twice daily continued as maintenance to reduce his craving for alcohol
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines have no role beyond managing withdrawal, and ongoing use risks dependence and precipitates encephalopathy in cirrhosis (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction Medicine).

options.text: Topiramate titrated slowly to 100 mg twice daily as first line relapse prevention
options.rationale: Topiramate has supportive evidence but is used off label in Australia and sits behind the registered agents when one of them is safe to give (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction Medicine).

options.text: Acamprosate 666 mg three times daily commenced now that withdrawal has resolved
options.rationale: Acamprosate is renally rather than hepatically cleared, which makes it the preferred agent in significant liver disease, and it supports maintenance of abstinence in a patient whose stated goal is complete abstinence (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction Medicine; Australian Medicines Handbook).

explanation.summary: Naltrexone and acamprosate are the two first line registered pharmacotherapies for alcohol use disorder in Australia, and the choice between them turns on organ function and on the patient's treatment goal. Naltrexone is hepatically metabolised and is preferred when the goal is reduced drinking rather than abstinence, since it blunts the reinforcing effect of alcohol that is drunk. Acamprosate is renally cleared and helps maintain abstinence once it has been achieved, which makes it the better fit for both the hepatic picture and the stated goal here. Both agents work best alongside psychosocial treatment, and neither is a substitute for it.
key_points: Naltrexone is hepatically metabolised and acamprosate is renally cleared
Acamprosate maintains abstinence once achieved, naltrexone reduces heavy drinking
Disulfiram is hepatotoxic and contraindicated in significant liver disease
Benzodiazepines have no maintenance role and precipitate encephalopathy in cirrhosis
explanation.pearls: Acamprosate needs a dose reduction once the estimated glomerular filtration rate falls below 60 mL/min and is contraindicated below 30, which is the mirror image of the hepatic limits that rule out naltrexone.

subtopic_detail: Substance induced depressive disorder versus independent major depression
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 39 year old man in the outpatient clinic, four weeks after an inpatient admission for alcohol withdrawal.

On admission he described eight months of low mood, hopelessness, poor sleep and thoughts that his family would be better off without him. Those eight months coincided exactly with an escalation from 10 to 30 standard drinks daily after he lost his job. He has now been continuously abstinent for four weeks, verified by carbohydrate deficient transferrin, and has taken no antidepressant at any stage. Today he reports that his mood, sleep, appetite and outlook have all returned to normal and he denies any suicidal thoughts. He had no depressive symptoms during a previous two year period of abstinence in his twenties.

data_table.Examination: Euthymic with reactive affect, no psychomotor change, no psychotic features
data_table.Investigations: Carbohydrate deficient transferrin within the abstinent range; liver function improving; thyroid function, full blood count and vitamin B12 within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Major depressive disorder in early remission following his recent hospital admission
options.rationale: Independent major depression does not reliably remit within four weeks of abstinence alone and without any antidepressant, and his previous abstinent period was symptom free (Source: American Psychiatric Association Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders Fifth Edition Text Revision).
source_refs: American Psychiatric Association Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders Fifth Edition Text Revision

options.text: Alcohol induced depressive disorder that has resolved with sustained abstinence
options.rationale: The symptoms began with the escalation in drinking, were absent during a previous prolonged abstinent period, and remitted within four weeks of abstinence without antidepressant treatment, which is the defining temporal signature (Source: American Psychiatric Association Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders Fifth Edition Text Revision).
source_refs: American Psychiatric Association Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders Fifth Edition Text Revision

options.text: Adjustment disorder with depressed mood precipitated by the loss of his employment
options.rationale: Adjustment disorder requires symptoms to resolve within six months of the stressor ending and does not accommodate eight months of symptoms of this severity including suicidal thinking (Source: American Psychiatric Association Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders Fifth Edition Text Revision).
source_refs: American Psychiatric Association Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders Fifth Edition Text Revision

options.text: Persistent depressive disorder with a superimposed alcohol use disorder developing
options.rationale: Persistent depressive disorder requires depressed mood for at least two years, whereas his symptoms lasted eight months and he was well through an earlier abstinent period (Source: American Psychiatric Association Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders Fifth Edition Text Revision).
source_refs: American Psychiatric Association Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders Fifth Edition Text Revision

options.text: Protracted alcohol withdrawal syndrome producing his ongoing affective disturbance
options.rationale: Protracted withdrawal would explain persisting symptoms rather than their complete resolution, and he is now entirely asymptomatic at four weeks (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction Medicine).

explanation.summary: Roughly 30 to 40 per cent of people presenting with depression and heavy alcohol use have a substance induced disorder rather than an independent one, and the distinction cannot be made at the first interview because the cross sectional picture is identical. Three pieces of longitudinal evidence separate them: whether symptoms preceded the substance use, whether they persisted during previous prolonged abstinence, and whether they remit with abstinence alone. Most substance induced depressive symptoms resolve within two to four weeks of abstinence, which is why a period of observation before committing to an antidepressant is standard rather than negligent. Persistence beyond about four weeks of verified abstinence redirects the diagnosis to an independent depressive disorder and prompts antidepressant treatment.
key_points: Substance induced depression is identical to independent depression cross sectionally
The separators are onset relative to use, symptoms during prior abstinence, and remission with abstinence
Most substance induced symptoms resolve within two to four weeks of abstinence
Persistence beyond four weeks of verified abstinence points to an independent disorder
explanation.pearls: Ask specifically about mood during any previous period of sustained abstinence, because a symptom free abstinent interval of months or years is the single most discriminating piece of history and is almost never volunteered.

sources.label: American Psychiatric Association Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders Fifth Edition Text Revision

subtopic_detail: Refeeding syndrome during inpatient nutritional rehabilitation
stem:
You are the medical registrar caring for a 19 year old woman admitted three days ago for nutritional rehabilitation. Her body mass index is 13.4 kg/m2 and she had eaten almost nothing for the preceding two weeks.

Nasogastric feeding was commenced on admission and she is now receiving 1400 kilocalories a day. She has taken thiamine and a multivitamin since admission. This morning she reports calf cramps and feels short of breath climbing one flight of stairs. Her chest is clear on auscultation, her jugular venous pressure is not elevated and there are no peripheral oedema or crackles. Her electrocardiogram shows a corrected QT interval of 470 ms.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 52, BP 96/60, RR 20, SpO2 98% room air, temperature 36.2
data_table.Examination: Chest clear, jugular venous pressure not elevated, no oedema, proximal weakness on standing from a chair
data_table.Investigations: Phosphate 0.38 mmol/L (0.75-1.50); potassium 3.0 mmol/L (3.5-5.2); magnesium 0.58 mmol/L (0.70-1.10); corrected QT interval 470 ms; creatinine and glucose within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Stop nasogastric feeding entirely and resume it once her electrolytes have normalised
options.rationale: Stopping nutrition in a severely malnourished patient causes further deterioration and prolongs the period of risk, and it is not what current guidance recommends for a correctable biochemical abnormality (Source: ANZAED and RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Eating Disorders).
source_refs: ANZAED and RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Eating Disorders

options.text: Increase her caloric intake as planned and repeat the electrolyte panel tomorrow
options.rationale: Escalating the caloric load drives further intracellular shift of phosphate, potassium and magnesium, and a 24 hour interval is far too long once the phosphate has already fallen this low (Source: ANZAED and RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Eating Disorders).
source_refs: ANZAED and RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Eating Disorders

options.text: Commence intravenous fluid resuscitation with normal saline and monitor her hourly
options.rationale: Sodium and volume loading risks precipitating cardiac failure in a myocardium that is atrophied and poorly compliant, and it does nothing about the electrolyte deficits driving her symptoms (Source: ANZAED and RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Eating Disorders).
source_refs: ANZAED and RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Eating Disorders

options.text: Continue feeding at a reduced rate and replace phosphate, potassium and magnesium
options.rationale: Refeeding syndrome is managed by slowing rather than ceasing nutrition while aggressively correcting the three electrolytes that shift intracellularly, with continuous cardiac monitoring given the prolonged corrected QT interval (Source: ANZAED and RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Eating Disorders; Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal).
source_refs: ANZAED and RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Eating Disorders

options.text: Replace phosphate alone and continue the current feeding rate without other changes
options.rationale: Correcting phosphate while leaving hypokalaemia and hypomagnesaemia untreated leaves the arrhythmia risk in place, and magnesium repletion is required before potassium will correct at all (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal).

explanation.summary: Refeeding syndrome arises when carbohydrate delivery to a starved patient triggers an insulin surge that drives phosphate, potassium and magnesium into cells, on top of total body stores that are already depleted. Phosphate depletion impairs adenosine triphosphate generation and red cell oxygen delivery, producing the weakness, breathlessness and cardiac dysfunction seen here. The historical response of stopping feeding has been superseded, because starvation itself is what the patient is being treated for, and current practice slows the rate while replacing electrolytes and continuing thiamine. Highest risk features include a body mass index below 14, negligible intake for more than five days, and low baseline electrolytes, all of which mandate cardiac monitoring and at least daily biochemistry during the first week.
key_points: Insulin driven intracellular shift of phosphate, potassium and magnesium is the mechanism
Slow the rate of feeding rather than stopping it and replace the electrolytes
Magnesium must be corrected before hypokalaemia will respond to potassium replacement
Thiamine is given before and throughout refeeding to prevent Wernicke encephalopathy
explanation.pearls: Check phosphate, potassium and magnesium at least daily for the first week of refeeding in anyone with a body mass index under 14, because the nadir typically falls on days two to four rather than on the day feeding starts.

sources.label: ANZAED and RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Eating Disorders

stem:
You are the registrar in a perinatal mental health clinic seeing a 32 year old woman who has just discovered she is seven weeks pregnant. The pregnancy is wanted and she intends to continue it.

She has bipolar I disorder with four previous manic episodes, two of which required involuntary admission and one of which followed an abrupt cessation of treatment. She has been well for five years on lithium carbonate 900 mg nightly and has never responded to any other agent. Her lithium level is 0.72 mmol/L, her renal and thyroid function are within normal limits, and she has no other medical history. She asks whether she should stop the lithium immediately.

data_table.Examination: Euthymic, insight intact, no psychotic features
data_table.Investigations: Serum lithium 0.72 mmol/L (0.6-0.8); creatinine, estimated glomerular filtration rate and thyroid function within normal limits; dating ultrasound consistent with seven weeks

lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice regarding her lithium?

options.text: Continue lithium with more frequent level monitoring and arrange a detailed cardiac scan
options.rationale: The absolute risk of Ebstein anomaly is roughly 1 in 1000 with first trimester lithium, which is far outweighed by a relapse risk above 50 per cent after cessation in a woman with four manic episodes and no alternative that has worked (Source: COPE Australian Clinical Practice Guideline for Perinatal Mental Health; RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Mood Disorders).
source_refs: COPE Australian Clinical Practice Guideline for Perinatal Mental Health
RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Mood Disorders

options.text: Cease lithium immediately and monitor her mental state weekly through the pregnancy
options.rationale: Abrupt cessation carries the highest relapse risk of any option and has already precipitated one manic episode in her history, and organogenesis is in any case well advanced by seven weeks (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Mood Disorders).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Mood Disorders

options.text: Cross taper lithium to sodium valproate over four weeks and monitor her levels
options.rationale: Valproate is the most teratogenic of all the mood stabilisers and swapping to it in pregnancy exchanges a small cardiac risk for a much larger malformation and neurodevelopmental risk (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Cross taper lithium to lamotrigine over four weeks and continue it through delivery
options.rationale: Lamotrigine protects mainly against depressive relapse and has weak evidence for mania prevention, so it is a poor substitute in an illness that has been consistently manic (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Mood Disorders).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Mood Disorders

options.text: Halve the lithium dose for the first trimester and restore the full dose afterwards
options.rationale: A subtherapeutic level leaves her exposed to the drug while removing its prophylactic effect, and the teratogenic association is with exposure rather than being reliably dose avoidable (Source: COPE Australian Clinical Practice Guideline for Perinatal Mental Health).
source_refs: COPE Australian Clinical Practice Guideline for Perinatal Mental Health

explanation.summary: The absolute teratogenic risk of first trimester lithium has been revised sharply downward from early registry estimates, with the risk of Ebstein anomaly now put at roughly 1 in 1000 against a background population rate of about 1 in 20000. That has to be weighed against relapse rates above 50 per cent when lithium is stopped in pregnancy, rising further with abrupt cessation, and against the consequences of mania in pregnancy for both mother and foetus. By seven weeks the cardiac outflow tract has already formed, so stopping now removes future protection without undoing past exposure. Practical management involves more frequent level monitoring as renal clearance rises through pregnancy, a foetal echocardiogram at around 18 to 20 weeks, and a plan to withhold or reduce the dose around labour when volume shifts make toxicity likely.
key_points: Ebstein anomaly risk with first trimester lithium is about 1 in 1000
Relapse risk after stopping lithium in pregnancy exceeds 50 per cent and rises with abrupt cessation
Cardiac organogenesis is complete by seven weeks, so stopping does not undo exposure
Renal clearance rises through pregnancy so levels need checking more often
explanation.pearls: Lithium clearance falls abruptly at delivery as plasma volume contracts, so withhold the dose at the onset of labour and recheck the level within 24 hours postpartum before restarting the pre pregnancy dose.

sources.label: COPE Australian Clinical Practice Guideline for Perinatal Mental Health
RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Mood Disorders

subtopic_detail: Serotonin toxicity after an antidepressant switch
stem:
You are the emergency registrar reviewing a 34 year old woman brought in by her partner with agitation and shaking that began six hours ago.

Her general practitioner stopped fluoxetine 40 mg daily last week and started tranylcypromine four days ago. She takes no other regular medication and no illicit substances. On examination her jaw is not rigid, her limbs move freely against gravity, and inducible clonus is present at both ankles with ocular clonus also seen. Her lower limb tone is markedly greater than her upper limb tone. Her creatine kinase is 620 U/L and she has had no recent antipsychotic exposure.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 126, BP 158/94, RR 26, SpO2 97% room air, temperature 38.6
data_table.Examination: Inducible ankle clonus, ocular clonus, hyperreflexia, lower limb tone greater than upper limb, diaphoresis, mydriasis
data_table.Investigations: Creatine kinase 620 U/L (30-190); sodium, potassium, creatinine and blood glucose within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Give dantrolene and bromocriptine and admit her to a critical care bed for cooling
options.rationale: These agents treat neuroleptic malignant syndrome, which is excluded by the absence of any antipsychotic exposure and by clonus and hyperreflexia rather than lead pipe rigidity and bradykinesia (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology).

options.text: Restart fluoxetine at a lower dose and continue tranylcypromine under observation
options.rationale: Reintroducing a serotonin reuptake inhibitor alongside a monoamine oxidase inhibitor is the interaction that caused this presentation and would make it substantially worse (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Cease both antidepressants, give benzodiazepines and add oral cyproheptadine
options.rationale: Withdrawal of the serotonergic agents with benzodiazepine sedation is the foundation of treatment, and cyproheptadine is the serotonin antagonist added when features are moderate to severe as they are with hyperthermia and clonus (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology; Austin Health Toxicology Handbook).

options.text: Give a single dose of intravenous haloperidol and observe her for two hours
options.rationale: Antipsychotics with dopamine blockade do not treat serotonin toxicity, impair heat dissipation and can convert the presentation into a mixed and more dangerous syndrome (Source: Austin Health Toxicology Handbook).

options.text: Give paracetamol for the fever and observe her overnight on the short stay unit
options.rationale: Hyperthermia here is generated by muscular hyperactivity rather than by a raised hypothalamic set point, so antipyretics are ineffective and ward observation underestimates the risk (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology).

explanation.summary: Serotonin toxicity is a clinical diagnosis made on the triad of neuromuscular excitation, autonomic instability and altered mental state, with the Hunter criteria resting heavily on clonus. It is separated from neuroleptic malignant syndrome by tempo and by the character of the motor findings, since serotonin toxicity develops within hours and produces clonus and hyperreflexia that are greater in the legs, while neuroleptic malignant syndrome evolves over days with generalised lead pipe rigidity and bradykinesia. Monoamine oxidase inhibitors combined with any serotonergic drug produce the most severe form, and fluoxetine's long half life means a washout of about five weeks is required before starting one. Treatment is withdrawal of the offending agents, benzodiazepines for agitation and rigidity, active cooling, and cyproheptadine for moderate to severe cases, with paralysis and intubation if hyperthermia exceeds 39 degrees.
key_points: Clonus, hyperreflexia and lower limb predominant hypertonia define serotonin toxicity
Onset within hours contrasts with the days long evolution of neuroleptic malignant syndrome
Fluoxetine requires about five weeks of washout before a monoamine oxidase inhibitor
Antipyretics do not work because the heat is generated by muscular activity
explanation.pearls: A temperature above 39 degrees in serotonin toxicity is an indication for immediate paralysis, intubation and active cooling rather than escalating drug therapy, because the hyperthermia itself causes rhabdomyolysis and disseminated intravascular coagulation within hours.

subtopic_detail: Clozapine induced myocarditis in the initiation window
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 25 year old man on day 18 of a clozapine titration for treatment resistant schizophrenia. He is now taking 250 mg daily and his psychotic symptoms have improved.

Over the past two days he has felt increasingly tired and short of breath walking to the dining room, which he could do comfortably last week. He has no cough, no pleuritic pain and no calf swelling. His neutrophil count has remained normal throughout and his chest radiograph shows no consolidation. His troponin and C reactive protein were both normal at baseline before clozapine was started.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 122, BP 104/64, RR 22, SpO2 96% room air, temperature 37.8
data_table.Examination: Chest clear on auscultation, no murmur, no calf tenderness, no rash
data_table.Investigations: Troponin I 340 ng/L (less than 16); C reactive protein 78 mg/L (less than 5); neutrophils 4.6 x10^9/L (2.0-7.5); eosinophils 0.9 x10^9/L (less than 0.5); chest radiograph clear

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Continue clozapine at the current dose and repeat the troponin again in 48 hours
options.rationale: Continuing the drug in the face of a rising troponin and C reactive protein risks progression to fulminant myocarditis and death, and a 48 hour delay is not a safe observation interval (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia

options.text: Halve the clozapine dose and arrange an outpatient echocardiogram within two weeks
options.rationale: Myocarditis is a hypersensitivity reaction that is not dose dependent, so halving the dose provides no protection and defers the investigation that decides management (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia

options.text: Withhold clozapine tonight and recommence the titration if he improves by morning
options.rationale: A single withheld dose followed by rechallenge exposes him again to the agent causing the reaction, and rechallenge after confirmed myocarditis is undertaken only in highly specialised settings (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Commence empirical intravenous antibiotics and continue the clozapine titration
options.rationale: The clear chest radiograph, normal neutrophil count and absence of a septic focus make bacterial infection unlikely, and treating it does not address the cardiac injury (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Cease clozapine immediately and arrange an urgent echocardiogram and cardiology review
options.rationale: Tachycardia, breathlessness and fever with a rising troponin, C reactive protein and eosinophil count between days 14 and 21 of titration is clozapine induced myocarditis until proven otherwise, and immediate cessation with urgent cardiac assessment is the standard response (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia; Australian Medicines Handbook).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia

explanation.summary: Clozapine induced myocarditis occurs in roughly 1 to 3 per cent of Australian patients and clusters tightly in the second and third weeks of titration, which is why many local protocols include baseline and weekly troponin and C reactive protein for the first four weeks. It is a hypersensitivity reaction rather than a dose dependent toxicity, and eosinophilia is a supportive feature. The early symptoms of fatigue, breathlessness, tachycardia and low grade fever are easily attributed to clozapine's known sedation or to an incidental viral illness, and that misattribution is the main cause of death. Neutrophil monitoring, which is mandatory and familiar, gives no protection against this complication at all, so a normal neutrophil count is falsely reassuring.
key_points: Myocarditis clusters between days 14 and 21 of clozapine titration
Baseline and weekly troponin and C reactive protein for the first four weeks are standard in Australia
It is a hypersensitivity reaction and is not dose dependent
A normal neutrophil count offers no reassurance about myocarditis
explanation.pearls: A persistent resting tachycardia above 120 beats per minute in the third week of clozapine titration warrants a troponin and C reactive protein the same day, even when the patient attributes the breathlessness to being unfit.

sources.label: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia

subtopic_detail: Empirical therapy for native valve infective endocarditis
stem:
You are the medical registrar admitting a 58 year old man with three weeks of fevers, night sweats and lethargy. He is a retired teacher with no prosthetic material, no indwelling lines and no injecting drug use, and he has not been in hospital or aged care in the past year.

He had a dental extraction six weeks ago. A new early diastolic murmur is audible at the left sternal edge and there are splinter haemorrhages in two nail beds. Three sets of blood cultures have been taken from separate sites and are pending. Transthoracic echocardiography shows a 9 mm mobile aortic valve vegetation with mild regurgitation. He has no penicillin allergy and his renal function is within normal limits.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 104, BP 118/58, RR 20, SpO2 97% room air, temperature 38.4
data_table.Examination: Early diastolic murmur at left sternal edge, splinter haemorrhages, no stigmata of injecting drug use
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 15.2 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0); C reactive protein 142 mg/L (less than 5); creatinine 78 micromol/L (60-110); echocardiogram shows 9 mm aortic vegetation

lead_in: Which empirical antibiotic regimen is the most appropriate to start now?

options.text: Ceftriaxone with oral rifampicin, awaiting blood culture results before escalation
options.rationale: Ceftriaxone alone lacks reliable staphylococcal cover, and rifampicin is added only for prosthetic material rather than for native valve disease (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Benzylpenicillin with flucloxacillin and gentamicin, adjusted once cultures return
options.rationale: This is the standard Australian empirical regimen for community acquired native valve endocarditis in a patient without penicillin allergy, covering viridans streptococci, staphylococci and enterococci while cultures are pending (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Vancomycin with gentamicin and rifampicin, adjusted once blood cultures return
options.rationale: This regimen is used for prosthetic valve endocarditis or where methicillin resistance is likely, and vancomycin is inferior to flucloxacillin for methicillin susceptible staphylococci (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Piperacillin with tazobactam, awaiting blood culture results before any escalation
options.rationale: Broad gram negative cover is unnecessary here and this combination gives no advantage against the organisms that actually cause native valve endocarditis (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Withhold all antibiotics until the blood culture results are available in 48 hours
options.rationale: Cultures have already been taken from three separate sites, and delaying treatment in a patient with a mobile vegetation and systemic sepsis risks embolic stroke and valve destruction (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

explanation.summary: The modified Duke criteria combine two major criteria, positive blood cultures with typical organisms and evidence of endocardial involvement, with minor criteria including fever, predisposition, vascular and immunological phenomena. Three sets of blood cultures from separate sites before antibiotics are the single highest yield investigation, and once they are taken empirical therapy should not be delayed. The Australian empirical regimen for community acquired native valve disease covers viridans streptococci, staphylococci and enterococci, and is narrowed as soon as an organism is identified. Vancomycin replaces the penicillins when there is immediate hypersensitivity to penicillin or a substantial risk of methicillin resistance, and rifampicin is reserved for prosthetic material.
key_points: Three sets of blood cultures from separate sites precede antibiotics but must not delay them
Native valve community acquired empirical cover targets streptococci, staphylococci and enterococci
Rifampicin is added for prosthetic material, not for native valve disease
Flucloxacillin outperforms vancomycin for methicillin susceptible staphylococci
explanation.pearls: A new regurgitant murmur counts as a major Duke criterion only when it is genuinely new, so an increase in the intensity of a previously documented murmur does not qualify and should not be used to reach the diagnosis.

sources.label: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand position statement

subtopic_detail: Timing of dexamethasone and antibiotics in adult bacterial meningitis
stem:
You are the emergency registrar assessing a 43 year old woman with 12 hours of severe headache, neck stiffness and photophobia. She is drowsy but obeys commands and has a Glasgow coma scale of 13.

Fundoscopy shows blurred disc margins in both eyes, so computed tomography of the head is required before lumbar puncture. The scanner is occupied and the radiographer estimates a 45 minute wait. Two sets of blood cultures have just been taken. She has no allergies, has not travelled overseas and is not immunosuppressed. There is no rash and her coagulation profile is within normal limits.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 112, BP 138/82, RR 22, SpO2 97% room air, temperature 38.9
data_table.Examination: Glasgow coma scale 13, neck stiffness, bilateral blurred disc margins, no focal deficit, no rash
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 19.8 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0); C reactive protein 210 mg/L (less than 5); coagulation profile and platelets within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Wait for the scan and lumbar puncture before starting any antimicrobial treatment
options.rationale: Every hour of delay to effective antibiotics increases mortality in bacterial meningitis, and cultures have already been taken so nothing is gained by waiting (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Give ceftriaxone now and add dexamethasone only if the culture grows pneumococcus
options.rationale: Dexamethasone must precede or accompany the first antibiotic dose to blunt the inflammatory response to bacterial lysis, so giving it days later on a culture result has no benefit (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Give ceftriaxone and benzylpenicillin now and add dexamethasone after the scan
options.rationale: Benzylpenicillin adds nothing to ceftriaxone in an immunocompetent adult of this age, and deferring the steroid until after the scan misses the window in which it works (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Give dexamethasone immediately followed by ceftriaxone, then proceed to the scan
options.rationale: Dexamethasone given with or just before the first antibiotic dose reduces mortality and hearing loss in pneumococcal meningitis, and neither is delayed for imaging once blood cultures have been taken (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Give aciclovir and dexamethasone now and defer antibacterial therapy until the scan
options.rationale: The febrile meningitic picture with a very high C reactive protein points to bacterial rather than viral disease, and antiviral cover does not substitute for antibacterial therapy (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

explanation.summary: Bacterial meningitis is a time critical diagnosis in which the sequence of investigations must never delay treatment, and the single decision that most affects outcome is how quickly the first antibiotic dose is given. Computed tomography before lumbar puncture is indicated for reduced conscious state, focal neurological signs, papilloedema, seizures or immunosuppression, and the scan is arranged after treatment has started, not before. Dexamethasone works by suppressing the cytokine surge that follows antibiotic induced bacterial lysis, so it must be given with or just before the first dose and has no benefit if delayed. Ceftriaxone is the empirical agent for immunocompetent adults, with benzylpenicillin added for listeria cover in patients over 50, in pregnancy, or where immunosuppression is present.
key_points: Antibiotics are never delayed for imaging once blood cultures are taken
Dexamethasone must be given with or just before the first antibiotic dose
Imaging before lumbar puncture is for reduced consciousness, focal signs, papilloedema, seizures or immunosuppression
Add benzylpenicillin for listeria cover over age 50, in pregnancy, or with immunosuppression
explanation.pearls: Cerebrospinal fluid culture yield falls substantially within an hour of the first antibiotic dose, but the cell count, protein, glucose and bacterial nucleic acid testing remain informative for days, so a delayed lumbar puncture is still worth doing.

sources.label: Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care sepsis standard

stem:
You are the registrar in an after hours general practice clinic. A 36 year old woman with primary adrenal insufficiency telephones and then attends with 10 hours of vomiting and watery diarrhoea after a family barbecue.

She normally takes hydrocortisone 20 mg in the morning and 10 mg in the afternoon, plus fludrocortisone 100 mcg daily. She doubled her morning hydrocortisone dose today but vomited within 20 minutes of taking it and has kept nothing down since. She feels dizzy on standing. Her capillary blood glucose is 3.9 mmol/L and her lying to standing blood pressure falls from 104/62 to 84/54 mmHg.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 108, BP 104/62 lying, RR 18, SpO2 98% room air, temperature 37.4
data_table.Examination: Dry mucous membranes, capillary refill 3 seconds, postural drop to 84/54 mmHg, alert and orientated
data_table.Investigations: Capillary blood glucose 3.9 mmol/L (3.0-7.7); point of care sodium 131 mmol/L (135-145); potassium 5.3 mmol/L (3.5-5.2)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Give hydrocortisone 100 mg by intramuscular injection and arrange urgent transfer
options.rationale: Vomiting makes oral replacement unreliable and the postural drop, hyponatraemia and hyperkalaemia signal an evolving adrenal crisis, so parenteral hydrocortisone is given immediately and before any transfer (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology; Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Give oral hydrocortisone 40 mg with an antiemetic and review her again in one hour
options.rationale: Any oral steroid dose is unreliable in a patient who has vomited repeatedly for 10 hours, and an hour of observation wastes the window in which crisis is reversible (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology).

options.text: Double her fludrocortisone dose and encourage oral rehydration solution at home
options.rationale: Fludrocortisone has minimal glucocorticoid activity and is redundant once high dose hydrocortisone is given, which itself provides ample mineralocorticoid effect (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Take a random serum cortisol and withhold steroid until the result is available
options.rationale: Treatment in a known adrenal insufficient patient is never delayed for biochemistry, and the diagnosis is already established so the cortisol adds nothing (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology).

options.text: Give intravenous normal saline alone and reassess her postural blood pressure hourly
options.rationale: Fluid corrects volume depletion but cannot replace the absent glucocorticoid, and saline alone will not reverse the hypoglycaemia or the vascular unresponsiveness (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology).

explanation.summary: Adrenal crisis is a leading preventable cause of death in primary adrenal insufficiency, and it is usually precipitated by an intercurrent illness during which oral replacement is either not increased or not absorbed. Sick day rules ask patients to double or triple oral hydrocortisone for fever or significant illness, and to use parenteral hydrocortisone whenever vomiting or diarrhoea prevents reliable absorption. Every patient should hold an emergency injection kit and a steroid alert card and should have been trained, along with a family member, to use it. The biochemical signature of hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia and hypoglycaemia supports the diagnosis but treatment always precedes confirmation in a patient already known to have the condition.
key_points: Double or triple oral hydrocortisone for fever or intercurrent illness
Vomiting or diarrhoea mandates parenteral hydrocortisone rather than oral dosing
Hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia and hypoglycaemia are the biochemical signature
Treatment is never delayed for a cortisol result in established disease
explanation.pearls: Hydrocortisone 100 mg has enough mineralocorticoid activity to make fludrocortisone unnecessary while the patient remains on high dose therapy, so it is restarted only once the daily hydrocortisone dose falls below about 50 mg.
